needs.text: Whether the respondents' arrangement with the three medical practitioners could constitute subletting, assignment, or other parting with possession of all or part of the subject-premises.
Whether any alleged subletting, assignment, or parting with possession occurred without the landlord's written consent.
Whether the tenant retained physical and legal control or the three medical practitioners obtained exclusive possession or control of a portion of the premises.

Whether the relevant alleged transfer conduct falls within the supplied statutory date and procedural requirements, including the post-9-June-1952 requirement and the prescribed section 14 recovery proceeding.

How the conflicting Rent Controller, Appellate Tribunal, and High Court findings concerning the doctors' occupation and the tenant's retained control connect to the fixed section 14(1)(b) issue without treating any lower-court conclusion as the withheld target outcome.

objects.text: Connaught Place shop room, the subject-premises
Dr. Pradip Jayna, Dr. S. S. Pant, and Shri K. N. Mehta, respondents 2-4
Mezzanine floor portion used for medical practice

facts.text: The landlord instituted an eviction proceeding under section 14 in 1974 concerning the subject-premises.
facts.speaker: NARRATOR
facts.stage: case history describing Rent Controller proceeding
unknown: whether the application satisfied every prescribed procedural requirement
facts.quote: The eviction proceeding was instituted in the year 1974.

facts.text: The appellant is admitted to be the landlord of the subject-premises.
facts.speaker: NARRATOR
facts.quote: The appellant admittedly is the landlord of the subject-premises.

facts.text: The landlord's principal eviction ground was alleged subletting without the landlord's consent.
facts.speaker: LANDLORD
unknown: whether lack of written consent was proved
whether statutory subletting or other parting with possession was proved
facts.quote: The main ground on which eviction was asked for was sub-letting without consent of the landlord.

facts.text: The landlord alleged that the respondents sublet portions of the premises to three medical practitioners and two firms.
facts.speaker: LANDLORD
unknown: whether the alleged portions were placed in exclusive possession
facts.quote: the respondents had sub-let certain portions of the premises to three medical practitioners

facts.text: The Additional Rent Controller found that the landlord had failed to show subletting, assignment, or parting with possession in favour of the impleaded persons or entities.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.stage: Additional Rent Controller decision dated 5 June 1997
facts.quote: the appellant had failed to show that there was any sub-letting, assignment or parting with possession

facts.text: The Rent Controller found that respondents 2 to 4 were not in exclusive possession of the subject-premises.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: 2 to 4 were not in exclusive possession of the subject- premises.

facts.text: The Appellate Tribunal reversed the first-instance decision and accepted the landlord's position that the facts disclosed subletting to respondents 2 to 4.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: The Tribunal accepted the appellant’s stand that the facts of the case disclosed sub- letting

facts.text: The landlord pressed the position that respondents 2 to 4 had been inducted as subtenants without the landlord's written consent.
facts.speaker: LANDLORD
facts.stage: position described in judgment under Supreme Court appeal
unknown: whether absence of written consent was independently found as fact
facts.quote: having been inducted as sub-tenants without the consent in writing by the landlord.

facts.text: The High Court found that the Tribunal's conclusion that respondents 2 to 4 had exclusive possession during clinic use was unsupported by evidence and based on surmises.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: the user of the space by R-2 to R-4 during the period they were in their respective clinic renders it they being in “exclusive possession” is not supported by any evidence

facts.text: The High Court found that the tenant had always remained in full physical and legal control and possession of the tenanted premises.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: the tenant has always been in full control and possession-physical and legal-of the tenanted premises.

facts.text: The High Court found that the others' presence was temporary, for a few hours while the tenant was also present, and was permissive use ending when the tenant called upon them to leave.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.quote: The presence of others was temporary, for a few hours of the day when the tenant would also be present, and clearly for permissive use

facts.text: The High Court set aside the Tribunal judgment, restored the Rent Controller judgment, and dismissed the eviction case at that stage.
facts.speaker: COURT
unknown: withheld outcome of the subsequent Supreme Court appeal
facts.quote: The judgment dated 05.06.1997 of the Additional Rent Controller stands restored and revived.

facts.text: In the Supreme Court appeal record, occupation of a portion of the premises by the three doctors is stated to stand admitted.
facts.speaker: COURT
unknown: legal character of the admitted occupation
scope of possession transferred, if any
facts.quote: occupation of a portion of the subject-premises by the three doctors stands admitted.

facts.text: The tenant respondents argued that full control was never ceded to the medical practitioners and that entry and exit remained under the tenant's exclusive control.
facts.speaker: TENANT
facts.quote: full control over the premises was never ceded to the medical practitioners

facts.text: In the retained Tribunal reasons, the Tribunal treated the doctors as being provided an exclusive mezzanine-floor portion without interference by the tenant.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.stage: Appellate Tribunal reasons quoted in Supreme Court record
facts.quote: in exclusive portion, i.e., Mezzanine floor without any interference even by the tenant.

facts.text: In the retained Tribunal reasons, the Tribunal treated the doctors' use of the mezzanine floor as exclusive during their permitted practice periods and treated that arrangement as more than a mere licence.
facts.speaker: COURT
facts.stage: Appellate Tribunal reasons quoted in Supreme Court record
facts.quote: user of the suit premises that too of Mezzanine floor was exclusive for the time they were permitted to run their practice

relations.text: The retained Tribunal reasoning treats the mezzanine floor used by the doctors as a portion of the suit premises.
relations.speaker: COURT
relations.stage: Appellate Tribunal reasons quoted in Supreme Court record
unknown: exact physical boundaries of the mezzanine portion

relations.text: The High Court found that the tenant retained full physical and legal control and possession of the tenanted premises.
relations.speaker: COURT
relations.quote: tenant has always been in full control and possession-physical and legal-of the tenanted premises.

relations.text: The Appellate Tribunal treated the doctors' mezzanine-floor use as exclusive for the periods when they were permitted to practise there.
relations.speaker: COURT
relations.stage: Appellate Tribunal reasons quoted in Supreme Court record
